paras: A health teacher claims that students who sleep more tend to score higher on quizzes.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the teacher's claim?
byHand: The claim compares more sleep with higher scores, so it needs a comparison across sleep groups. A compares the least-sleep group (12.4) with the most-sleep group (16.5). Distractors: B and D give only one group's score, and C describes the quiz itself.
choices: Students who slept under 6 hours averaged 12.4; those who slept over 8 averaged 16.5.
Students who slept 7 to 8 hours averaged 16.1 on the quiz, out of a possible 20 points.
The quiz was scored out of 20 points, and 120 students in all took part in the study.
Students who slept 6 to 7 hours averaged a score just below 15, at 14.8 out of 20 points.

passage.caption: Seeds Sprouted After Two Weeks

paras: A student planted 50 bean seeds in each of three soil types and counted how many sprouted after two weeks. The student concluded that loam was the best soil for sprouting bean seeds, since ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
byHand: To support the conclusion that loam is best, the data must show loam outperformed both other soils. D does that (41 versus 26 and 18). Distractors: A describes the setup, B compares the other two soils, and C gives only the sandy-soil result.
choices: 50 seeds were planted in each of the three types of soil.
more seeds sprouted in clay than in sandy soil, 26 compared with 18.
only 18 of the 50 seeds planted in sandy soil sprouted after two weeks.
41 loam seeds sprouted, more than in either other soil.

passage.title: Percentage of Households with Internet Access in Country Z
passage.label: Percent of households

paras: Internet access in Country Z expanded rapidly in the early twenty-first century. Between 2000 and 2020, the percentage of households with internet access ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the text?
byHand: The text describes the change from 2000 to 2020. The graph shows 22 percent in 2000 and 88 percent in 2020, so C is right. Distractors: A ignores the change, B reverses it, and D describes only 2005 to 2010.

passage.caption: Results of a Survey on Preferred Lunch Options (300 Students)

paras: The student council surveyed 300 students about their preferred lunch option. The council reported that the hot meal was the most popular choice, ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
byHand: Calling the hot meal most popular requires showing it got more votes than each other option. D gives its total (135) and makes that comparison. Distractors: A and C give totals for other options, and B doesn't address popularity.
choices: since 72 students, fewer than a quarter of those surveyed, preferred the salad bar.
since every one of the 300 students surveyed chose one of the three options.
since 93 students preferred sandwiches, which is more than preferred the salad bar.
since 135 students chose it, more than chose either other option.

passage.caption: Average Monthly Rainfall in Two Cities (millimeters)

paras: A geography class compared summer rainfall in two cities. They found that in every summer month shown, Port Alma received far more rain than Desert Springs. In July, for instance, ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
byHand: The example should give July data showing Port Alma received far more rain than Desert Springs. C compares the two cities in July (110 versus 2). Distractors: A gives August figures, and B gives a June figure for only one city; D is false for Desert Springs, which got less rain in July (2) than in June (4).
choices: Desert Springs received 7 millimeters of rain, far less than Port Alma's 96.
Port Alma received 85 millimeters of rain, its lowest total of the three months.
Port Alma received 110 millimeters of rain, but Desert Springs only 2.
both cities received more rain than in June.

passage.title: Number of Monarch Butterflies Counted at a Nature Reserve
passage.label: Butterflies counted

paras: Volunteers at a nature reserve have counted monarch butterflies every fall since 2018. The counts suggest that the reserve's monarch population is declining: ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the text?
byHand: The text claims the population is declining, so the best support shows the drop across the years. A shows a fall each year from 3,400 to 1,600. Distractors: B gives a single year; C compares only two years; D doesn't show a decline.
choices: the count fell every year, from 3,400 in 2018 to 1,600 in 2021.
the count was higher in 2020 than in 2021.
more than 1,000 butterflies were counted every year.

passage.caption: Average Commute Time and Method in Four Cities (minutes)

paras: Urban planner Dana Liu notes that in some cities, public transit is the faster choice for commuters compared with driving. She points to Marlow and Westbrook as examples, where ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
byHand: Liu's point is that transit can beat driving. In Marlow (30 versus 34) and Westbrook (29 versus 31), the average transit commute is shorter than the car commute, so B is right. Distractors: A and D compare bicycles, which isn't her point; C is true but doesn't compare transit with driving.
choices: bicycle commutes are shorter on average than both car and transit commutes.
the average transit commute is shorter than the average car commute.
the average car commute is more than 30 minutes, longer than in Carlton or Penhurst.
public transit commutes are longer on average than bicycle commutes in each city.

passage.title: Percentage of Seedlings Surviving One Year, by Planting Method
passage.label: Percent surviving

paras: A forestry team tested two methods of replanting burned land: scattering seeds directly on the ground or planting young trees raised in a nursery. The team concluded that nursery seedlings survived better than direct seeding in every region tested, though survival also varied by location. For example, on the south slope, ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the example?
byHand: The example should show, for the south slope, that nursery seedlings survived better than direct seeding. D compares the two methods there (54 versus 18 percent). Distractors: A compares regions, not methods; B compares the south slope with the valley; C gives the valley's rate.
choices: 18 percent of directly seeded trees survived, compared with 31 percent on the north slope.
survival rates were lower than in the valley for both methods.
nursery seedlings had a survival rate of 72 percent.
54 percent of nursery seedlings survived, compared with only 18 percent of directly seeded trees.

passage.caption: Species Observed at Four Wetland Sites

paras: Ecologist Tariq Aziz argues that a wetland's size does not reliably predict how many species it supports. He notes that Site 3 had the most bird and amphibian species even though ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
byHand: Aziz argues size doesn't predict species counts, so the completion should contrast Site 3's high species counts with its relatively small size. Site 3 (18 hectares) was smaller than Sites 2 (30) and 4 (25), so C is right. Distractors: B emphasizes that Site 3 was larger than another site, which wouldn't support his point; A and D don't address Site 3's size.
choices: Site 1 had fewer amphibian species than Site 2.
it covered 18 hectares, more than Site 1.
it was smaller than both Site 2 and Site 4.
Site 4 had the fewest bird species of any site.

passage.caption: Share of Electricity Generated from Wind in Country R (percent)

paras: An energy analyst writes that wind power in Country R grew steadily during the 2010s and that its share of electricity more than quintupled between 2012 and 2020.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the analyst's claim?
byHand: The claim has two parts: steady growth, and a more than fivefold increase from 2012 to 2020. C shows growth in every year shown and the rise from 4 to 22 percent (more than five times 4). Distractors: A gives one year, B covers only the last two years, and D covers only the first two.
choices: Wind generated 11 percent of Country R's electricity in 2016.
Wind's share increased from 16 percent in 2018 to 22 percent in 2020.
Wind's share rose in every year shown, from 4 percent in 2012 to 22 percent in 2020.
Wind generated more electricity in 2014 than in 2012.

passage.title: Average Number of Words Recalled After Studying a List
passage.label: Words recalled (out of 30)

paras: Psychologists compared two study methods. Students who reread a word list remembered slightly more words when tested immediately, but students who tested themselves remembered far more a week later. The researchers concluded that self-testing produces more lasting learning, since after one week, ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
byHand: The conclusion is about lasting learning, so it needs the one-week results comparing the groups. B gives them: 14 for self-testers versus 7 for rereaders. Distractors: A and C give immediate results; D is true but doesn't show which method lasted better.
choices: students who reread the list recalled 18 words.
self-testers recalled 14 words on average, while rereaders recalled only 7.
self-testers recalled 17 words, almost as many as rereaders.
both groups recalled fewer words than they had immediately after studying.

passage.caption: Survey of 500 Adults: Main Source of News

paras: A media researcher observed that the role of social media as a news source differed sharply across age groups, while the share relying on print or websites was fairly similar for all ages. For example, ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to illustrate the researcher's observation?
byHand: The observation has two parts: big differences in social media use and similar shares for print or websites. B covers both. Distractors: A concerns television; C compares two sources within one group; D also concerns television.
choices: 61 percent of adults 65 and older relied mainly on television, compared with only 18 percent of adults aged 18–29, a gap of 43 points.
social media use ranged from 52 percent (ages 18–29) to 9 percent (65 and older), but print or websites only from 30 to 34 percent.
adults aged 30–49 were about equally likely to rely on social media (37 percent) and on print or websites (34 percent), unlike other groups.
adults aged 50–64 relied on television more than on any other source.

passage.caption: Average Height (cm) of Sunflowers Grown Under Different Light Conditions

paras: A student hypothesized that sunflowers grown with more light would not only be taller but would also grow faster over time, so that the difference between conditions would widen each week.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student's hypothesis?
byHand: The hypothesis predicts a widening difference between conditions. A shows the gap between full sun and full shade growing from 5 cm (14 − 9) to 74 cm (104 − 30). Distractors: C gives one measurement, B gives only the first week, and D describes one condition without a comparison.
choices: The gap between full sun and full shade grew from 5 centimeters at week 2 to 74 at week 8.
At week 2, sunflowers in full shade averaged 9 centimeters, compared with 14 in full sun.
At week 8, sunflowers in full sun averaged 104 centimeters, the tallest of any condition in any week.
Sunflowers in partial shade grew taller every week.

passage.title: Average Price of One Kilogram of Coffee Beans at Market
passage.label: US dollars

paras: A coffee cooperative's report states that after falling for two consecutive years, the market price of coffee beans began to recover, eventually exceeding its 2016 level.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the report's statement?
byHand: The statement describes two years of decline, a recovery, and a final price above 2016's. D covers all of that: down from $3.10 to $2.60, then up to $3.40. Distractors: A shows only the two years of decline; B shows only part of the recovery; C gives only the low point.
choices: The price was $3.10 per kilogram in 2016, then fell to $2.85 in 2017 and $2.60 in 2018.
The price was higher in 2019 than in 2018, rising from $2.60 to $2.70 per kilogram.
The price fell from $3.10 in 2016 to $2.60 in 2018, then rose to $3.40 by 2020.

passage.caption: Number of Bee Visits to Flowers in One Hour

paras: A biology student claims that bumblebees are more attracted to red flowers than honeybees are.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student's claim?
byHand: The claim compares the two kinds of bees' visits to red flowers. B gives that comparison: 15 bumblebee visits versus 4 honeybee visits. Distractors: A and D concern only honeybees and other colors; C compares bumblebee visits across colors, which would seem to weaken the claim rather than support it.
choices: Honeybees visited blue flowers 46 times, more than any other color.
Bumblebees visited red flowers 15 times, while honeybees visited them only 4 times.
Bumblebees visited blue flowers more than red flowers.

passage.caption: Library Program Attendance Before and After Moving Programs to Evenings

paras: After a library moved most of its programs from afternoons to evenings, attendance rose for most programs, though not for all of them. The ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
byHand: The final sentence follows "though not for all of them," so it should give an example of a program whose attendance didn't rise. The craft workshop fell from 18 to 16, so C is right. Distractors: A, B, and D all describe programs that grew.
choices: film night drew the most people in both time slots, with 30 in the afternoon and 41 in the evening.
coding class's attendance nearly tripled, rising from 9 to 25.
craft workshop, for example, averaged 18 people in the afternoon but only 16 in the evening.
book club grew from 14 people to 22 people.

passage.title: Average Lifespan in Captivity and in the Wild
passage.label: Years

paras: A zoologist explains that animals don't always live longer in captivity, even with veterinary care and steady food. Some large, wide-ranging species, she notes, have far shorter lives in captivity than in the wild, as the ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the text?
byHand: The completion needs a large, wide-ranging species that lives far less in captivity. The African elephant lives about 56 years in the wild but 17 in captivity, so B is right. Distractors: A and C describe animals that live longer in captivity; D doesn't compare captivity with the wild.
choices: gray wolf shows, living about 14 years in captivity but only about 6 years in the wild.
African elephant shows, living about 56 years in the wild but 17 in captivity.
red fox shows, living about 3 years in the wild but about 12 years in captivity.
orca and gray wolf show, both living about 15 years in captivity.

passage.caption: Rates of a Plant Disease in Three Orchards Before and After Pruning Program (percent of trees infected)

paras: An agricultural scientist introduced a pruning program to reduce a plant disease in three orchards. The East orchard, however, began the program a year later than the others. The scientist concluded that the program was likely effective, noting that infection rates fell sharply in the orchards that followed it for the full two years, whereas ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
byHand: "Whereas" signals a contrast with the orchards that had the full program, so the completion should describe the East orchard, which started late. Its rate barely changed (28 to 26 percent), which C states. Distractors: A and B describe orchards that had the full program; D is true, but it doesn't make the contrast the scientist draws.
choices: the South orchard had the highest infection rate of the three orchards before the program began.
the North orchard's infection rate fell from 34 percent in 2019 to just 12 percent in 2021.
the East orchard's rate, after less time in the program, barely changed: 28 to 26 percent.
all three orchards had infection rates below 30 percent in 2021, after the pruning program.

passage.caption: Average Test Scores by Number of Practice Sessions Attended

paras: A tutoring center reports that students who attended more practice sessions tended to score higher, but that the gains leveled off: attending five or more sessions was associated with little improvement over attending three or four.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support both parts of the center's report?
byHand: The report makes two points: scores rise with more sessions, and the gain levels off after three or four. C supports both, rising from 68 to 79 and then only to 80. Distractors: A and D show only the increase; B concerns how many students were in a group.
choices: Students who attended 0 sessions averaged 68, and students who attended 1–2 sessions averaged 71.
Only 17 students attended five or more sessions, the fewest of any group.
Average scores rose from 68 with no sessions to 79 with three or four, but only to 80 with five or more.
Students who attended 3–4 sessions averaged 79, which was 11 points higher than students who attended none.

passage.title: Percentage of Respondents Who Trust Local and National News
passage.label: Percent who trust

paras: A journalism professor argues that while trust in news has fallen overall, the decline has been concentrated in national news, with trust in local news remaining comparatively stable.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the professor's argument?
byHand: The argument contrasts a large drop in trust in national news with relative stability for local news. D gives both changes: a 24-point drop for national news and a 6-point drop for local news. Distractors: A gives only one year; C compares levels, not changes; B covers only national news over four years.
choices: In 2008, 72 percent of respondents trusted local news and 60 percent trusted national news, a gap of 12 percentage points.
Trust in national news fell by 9 percentage points between 2008 and 2012.
Trust in local news was higher than trust in national news in every year shown.
From 2008 to 2020, trust in national news fell from 60 to 36 percent, but trust in local news fell only from 72 to 66.

passage.caption: Nesting Success of Sea Turtles on Two Beaches

paras: Conservationists suspect that bright lights from buildings disorient sea turtle hatchlings and reduce nesting success. Comparing two beaches with a similar number of nests, they found that ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the conservationists' suspicion?
byHand: To support the suspicion, the data should show lower success where there are lights. A compares success rates: 96 of 120 (80 percent) at the unlit beach versus 58 of 115 (about 50 percent) at the lit beach. Distractors: C and D compare nest counts; B gives Harbor Point's results without a comparison.
choices: about 80 percent of nests at unlit Coral Bay produced hatchlings, compared with about 50 percent at lit Harbor Point.
Harbor Point, which has artificial lights nearby, had 58 nests with hatchlings out of the 115 nests counted on its beach that season.
Coral Bay had 120 nests, slightly more than Harbor Point's 115.
both beaches had more than 100 nests in the season studied.

passage.caption: Sales of a Phone Model, by Region (thousands of units)

paras: A company analyst claims that the phone model's sales grew in some regions and declined in others between Quarter 1 and Quarter 3, so overall sales changed little. She notes that growth in the North and East was largely offset by declines elsewhere: ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
byHand: After the colon, the analyst should name the declines that offset growth in the North and East. A describes the drops in the South and West. Distractors: C and D describe growth regions; B gives a single quarter's ranking, not a decline.
choices: sales fell from 60,000 to 51,000 units in the South and from 50,000 to 49,000 in the West.
the South had the highest sales of any region in Quarter 1.
sales in the North grew steadily from 42,000 units in Quarter 1 to 55,000 units in Quarter 3.
sales in the East grew in every quarter shown, rising from 35,000 to 47,000 units.

passage.caption: Percentage of Participants Who Completed a Twelve-Week Exercise Program

paras: A health researcher claims that exercising with other people, whether with a partner or in a class, makes people more likely to stick with an exercise program than exercising alone.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researcher's claim?
byHand: The claim compares both social options with exercising alone. A compares partner and class completion rates with the rate for those exercising alone. Distractors: C gives one group; B compares the two social groups to each other; D describes the setup.
choices: Participants with a partner (70 percent) and in a class (66 percent) both finished more often than those alone (45 percent).
Participants who exercised with a partner were slightly more likely to finish the program than those in a class, 70 percent to 66 percent.
70 percent of participants who exercised with a partner completed the program.

passage.title: Average Annual Snowfall at a Mountain Weather Station
passage.label: Centimeters

paras: A climatologist notes that snowfall at a mountain weather station has decreased in every decade since the 1970s and that the decline has accelerated: the drop from the 2000s to the 2010s was ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
byHand: Acceleration means the most recent drop is the largest. From the 2000s (330) to the 2010s (284) the drop was 46 cm, larger than the earlier drops of 15, 33, and 32 cm, so B is right. Distractors: A has the wrong value; C confuses the 2010s total with the drop; D gives the total decline since the 1970s, not the most recent drop.
choices: about 15 centimeters, the same as the drop from the 1970s to the 1980s.
about 46 centimeters, larger than the drop between any two earlier decades shown.
about 284 centimeters, the lowest snowfall recorded.
about 126 centimeters, the total decline since the 1970s.

passage.caption: Reading Scores Before and After a Summer Reading Program

paras: Educators often worry that students' reading skills slip over the summer. A school district found that students who joined its summer reading program ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
byHand: The context is summer learning loss, so the completion should show that program students avoided the slip that others experienced. A shows program students improving while others declined. Distractors: C and D are true but don't make that comparison; B is false (64 versus 70).
choices: improved their average from 72 to 76, while other students' average fell from 74 to 71.
outnumbered the students who did not join the program.
started the summer with lower average scores, 72 compared with 74, than students who did not join.
had an average September score of 76.

passage.caption: Pollinator Visits per Hour in Three Garden Plots

paras: A gardener hypothesizes that increasing the percentage of native plants in a plot will increase visits from both bees and butterflies.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the gardener's hypothesis?
byHand: The hypothesis links more native plants to more visits from both bees and butterflies. D shows both increasing across plots as the share of native plants rises. Distractors: A gives one plot's bee visits; B compares bees and butterflies within one plot; C gives one plot's butterfly visits.
choices: Plot C, which had 80 percent native plants, received 52 bee visits per hour, more than either of the other plots.
Plot B, with 50 percent native plants, received more bee visits (31) than butterfly visits (9) per hour.
Plot A, which had only 20 percent native plants, received the fewest butterfly visits per hour of any plot.
As native plants rose from 20 to 80 percent, bee visits rose from 14 to 52 and butterfly visits from 3 to 18.

passage.caption: Wildfire Area Burned and Prescribed Burns in Region Q
header: Acres treated with prescribed burns (per year)

paras: Forest managers in Region Q began expanding prescribed burns, small fires set on purpose to clear dry brush, in the early 2000s. A report argues that the program may have reduced wildfire damage, though it cautions that other factors, such as weather, could also have played a role. The report notes that ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the report's argument?
byHand: The report argues that prescribed burns may have reduced wildfire damage, so the evidence should show wildfire area falling as burns increased. D shows that pattern. Distractors: A and B each describe only one period; C is false for 2015–2019, when treated acres (26,000) exceeded burned acres (17,000).
choices: prescribed burns treated only 2,000 acres per year in the early 2000s, when wildfires burned 41,000 acres per year.
wildfires burned 22,000 acres per year from 2010 to 2014.
the area burned by wildfire was always larger than the area treated with prescribed burns in every period shown.
as prescribed burns rose from 2,000 to 26,000 acres per year, wildfire area fell from 41,000 to 17,000.

passage.caption: Average Temperature Inside Three Types of Bird Boxes on a Summer Afternoon

paras: Volunteers who build bird boxes for a wildlife group wanted to know which material keeps the boxes coolest in summer. They placed boxes made of three materials in the same sunny spot and measured the temperature inside. They recommended thick wood, since the wooden boxes ______

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
byHand: The volunteers wanted the coolest material, so the completion should show that wood was cooler than both alternatives. A does that. Distractors: D gives the plastic boxes' temperature; B introduces cost, which the table doesn't show; C reverses the data.
choices: averaged 29°C inside, cooler than both the plastic and metal boxes.
were the most expensive of the three materials that the group tested.
were warmer inside than the thin metal boxes placed in the same sunny spot.
reached an average of 36°C inside, the same as the boxes made of plastic.

paras: Biologist Hana Osei suspects that city-dwelling crows are bolder than crows in rural areas. She hypothesizes that because city crows encounter people constantly, they have learned that most humans pose no threat.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Osei's hypothesis?
byHand: Osei's hypothesis is that city crows are bolder around people because they've learned humans are mostly harmless. If city crows let people come much closer before fleeing, that directly supports it, so A is right. Distractors: B and C describe differences unrelated to boldness toward people; D concerns reactions to hawks, not humans.
choices: City crows allow people to approach much more closely before flying away than rural crows do.
Rural crows build their nests higher in trees than city crows do.
City crows eat a wider variety of foods than rural crows do.
Rural crows and city crows make similar alarm calls when they see a hawk.

paras: In her poem "Harbor Morning," the poet Celia Brandt portrays the sea as calm and welcoming, comparing it to something familiar and comforting.

stem: Which quotation from "Harbor Morning" most effectively illustrates the claim?
byHand: The claim says the sea is portrayed as calm and compared to something familiar and comforting. A blanket folded on a bed is exactly such a comparison, so B is right. Distractors: A describes gulls and "breaking" water, C describes a gathering storm, and D focuses on the fishermen's labor. None compares the sea to something comforting.
choices: "The gulls cry out above the breaking wall"
"The water folds itself like a blanket on a bed"
"Far off, the storm clouds gather at the edge"
"The fishermen haul their nets with aching arms"

paras: A team of researchers claims that playing music for tomato plants does not make them grow faster. To test this, they grew two groups of tomato plants in identical conditions, except that one group heard music for several hours each day.

stem: Which finding from the experiment, if true, would most directly support the researchers' claim?
byHand: If music doesn't make plants grow faster, the two groups should grow at about the same rate. C reports exactly that. Distractors: A suggests music had an effect; B describes a difference in growth over time, which doesn't clearly support the claim; D concerns water use, not growth.
choices: The plants that heard music produced more flowers than the other plants did.
The plants that heard music grew more slowly at first but caught up later.
Both groups of plants grew to nearly the same height over the same period.
The plants that did not hear music needed more water than the other plants did.

paras: Historian Lucas Ferreira argues that letters written by soldiers during the US Civil War show that many soldiers were deeply homesick.

stem: Which quotation from a soldier's letter would most directly support Ferreira's argument?
byHand: Ferreira argues that soldiers were homesick. C expresses constant longing for home, so it directly supports him. Distractors: A, B, and D describe marching, supplies, and food, none of which shows homesickness.
choices: "We marched twenty miles today and made camp by the river just as the sun went down."
"The officers say we will receive new boots and warmer coats before the winter sets in."
"Not an hour goes by that I do not think of you all at home and wish I were there."
"The food here is poor, but there is plenty of it, and no man in our company goes hungry."

paras: Nutrition researcher Dev Kapoor hypothesizes that students who eat breakfast are better able to concentrate during morning classes than students who skip breakfast.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Kapoor's hypothesis?
byHand: Kapoor predicts that breakfast eaters concentrate better in the morning. If breakfast skippers did just as well on attention tests, that undercuts the prediction, so D is right. Distractors: A, C, and B describe hunger, punctuality, and lunch size, which don't test concentration.
choices: Students who ate breakfast reported feeling less hungry before lunch.
Students who skipped breakfast ate larger lunches than students who ate breakfast.
Students who ate breakfast were more likely to arrive at school on time.
Students who skipped breakfast scored as well on morning attention tests as students who ate breakfast.

passage.text: The following text is from a novel. Mara has just started a new job at a bakery.

paras: In the novel, Mara is presented as someone who takes great care with her work, even with small tasks.

stem: Which quotation from the novel most effectively illustrates the claim?
byHand: The claim is that Mara is careful even with small tasks. Measuring salt twice and leveling each spoonful shows such care, so D is right. Distractors: A shows she arrives early, not that she works carefully; C describes the street and customers; B reports what her manager said.
choices: "Mara arrived at the bakery before sunrise each morning, yawning as she unlocked the heavy front door."
"Her manager told her that the shop would be busy on Saturday."
"The smell of fresh bread filled the street, and by seven o'clock customers had begun to line up outside the door."
"She measured each spoonful of salt twice, leveling it with a knife before tipping it in."

paras: Ecologist Ingrid Solberg claims that beavers can help reduce the damage caused by wildfires. She points out that beaver dams spread water across nearby land, creating wet areas that are harder for fire to burn.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Solberg's claim?
byHand: Solberg claims beaver dams create wet areas that resist fire. If land near dams stayed green while nearby areas burned, that directly supports her claim, so C is right. Distractors: A and D concern beaver behavior, not fire; B is a general point about dry regions that says nothing about beavers.
choices: Beavers build dams more quickly in the spring, when streams are high, than in the fall.
Wildfires tend to be more common and to burn longer in dry regions than in wet regions.
After a large fire, land near beaver dams stayed green while nearby areas burned.
Beavers often leave their dams and move to new streams after their food supply runs low.

paras: In the short story "The Lantern," the narrator's grandfather is portrayed as someone who is patient with children.

stem: Which quotation from "The Lantern" most effectively illustrates the claim?
byHand: Answering a child's question a tenth time with a smile shows patience with children, so D illustrates the claim. Distractors: A shows his skill, B his habits, and C describes his workshop.
choices: "My grandfather built the lantern himself from tin and colored glass, working late into the night."
"He walked to town every Sunday, rain or shine, and always came home before dark."
"His workshop smelled of oil and sawdust, and every tool hung in its proper place on the wall."
"When I asked the same question a tenth time, he just smiled and answered it again."

paras: A city transportation department claims that adding protected bike lanes to Main Street made the street safer for cyclists.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the department's claim?
byHand: The claim is that the lanes made Main Street safer for cyclists. A drop in cyclist crashes after the lanes were added directly supports it, so B is right. Distractors: A concerns car traffic, C suggests cyclists avoided the street, and D concerns cost.
choices: More cars used Main Street after the bike lanes were added than before.
Cyclist crashes on Main Street fell after the bike lanes were added.
Many cyclists said they preferred riding on quieter side streets instead of Main Street.
The bike lanes cost less to build than the department had expected when it planned them.

paras: Astronomer Felix Grant hypothesizes that a distant star dims regularly because a large planet passes in front of it on a fixed orbit.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Grant's hypothesis?
byHand: A planet on a fixed orbit would block the star's light on a regular schedule for the same duration each pass. B describes that pattern. Distractors: C would weaken the hypothesis; A and D say nothing about what causes the dimming.
choices: The star is brighter and larger than most of the other stars in its region of the sky.
The star dims at the same interval each time, for the same length of time.
The star dims at random times that cannot be predicted from its past behavior.
Several stars near this one have been observed closely and have no planets at all.

paras: Linguist Rosa Medina claims that young children often learn new words by watching where adults are looking when they speak.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Medina's claim?
byHand: Medina's claim connects word learning to where adults look. D shows children linking a new word to the object the adult was looking at, which supports the claim directly. Distractors: A, C, and B concern other influences on vocabulary and say nothing about adults' gaze.
choices: Children learn more words when they live in homes with many books and read with adults often.
Young children usually learn to say "mama" before they learn most other words, regardless of language.
Children often repeat words they hear on television, even words they don't yet understand.
When an adult looked at a new object while naming it, children linked the word to that object.

paras: Anthropologist Kwame Mensah argues that the market women of 1950s Accra, Ghana, held significant political influence. He notes that these traders controlled much of the city's food supply and formed associations that could organize collective action.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Mensah's argument?
byHand: Mensah claims the market women had political influence. If candidates regularly sought their associations' endorsement, that shows political power, so C is right. Distractors: A, B, and D describe the women's goods, training, and the market's size, which don't show political influence.
choices: Many market women in 1950s Accra sold cloth as well as food.
Most market women in 1950s Accra had learned their trade from relatives.
Political candidates in 1950s Accra regularly sought the endorsement of market women's associations.
Accra's central market grew larger in the 1950s than it had been in the 1940s.

passage.text: The following text is from a novel. Hilda Lund runs her family's farm on the prairie.

paras: In the novel, Hilda is portrayed as having a deep, almost spiritual connection to the land she farms.

stem: Which quotation from the novel most effectively illustrates the claim?
byHand: The claim is about a deep, almost spiritual bond with the land. C describes Hilda feeling that her heart is hidden in the land among its wild creatures, which conveys that bond. Distractors: A describes hardship, B her brothers' wishes, and D a routine errand.
choices: "She had a good many troubles that year, and the crops were poor."
"Her brothers wanted to sell the farm and move to the river towns."
"She felt as if her heart were hiding down there, somewhere, with the quail and the plover and all the little wild things that crooned or buzzed in the sun."
"She drove to town on Saturdays to buy supplies and hear the news."

paras: Psychologist Ines Albrecht hypothesizes that people remember information better when they explain it aloud to someone else than when they simply reread it. She asked two groups of students to study the same science passage, one by rereading and the other by explaining it to a partner.

stem: Which finding from Albrecht's study, if true, would most directly support her hypothesis?
byHand: The hypothesis compares memory after explaining with memory after rereading. A shows the explaining group recalled more a week later, directly supporting it. Distractors: B concerns study time, C concerns perceived difficulty, and D only describes the explaining group, so none compares memory.
choices: A week later, students who explained the passage recalled more key points than those who reread it.
Students in the rereading group spent more total time with the passage.
Students in both groups said that the passage was difficult to understand.
Students who explained the passage to a partner talked for an average of ten minutes about its main ideas.

paras: Some historians have argued that the Silk Road was mainly a route for luxury goods like silk and spices. Archaeologist Mei Tanaka disagrees, arguing that ordinary goods such as grain, pottery, and tools made up a large share of the trade.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Tanaka's argument?
byHand: Tanaka argues that ordinary goods made up a large share of Silk Road trade. Records listing everyday goods far more often than luxuries directly support that, so A is right. Distractors: C and B focus on luxury goods and would fit the view she opposes; D is about how merchants traveled, not what they traded.
choices: Records from several Silk Road trading posts list everyday goods far more often than luxury goods.
Spices traded along the Silk Road were often worth more than their weight in silver.
Silk found at a Silk Road trading post was made with an unusually complex weaving technique.
Merchants on the Silk Road often traveled in large groups for protection.

paras: Marine biologist Owen Hale claims that octopuses can recognize individual humans. He notes that octopuses in his lab behave differently toward different caretakers, even when the caretakers wear identical uniforms.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Hale's claim?
byHand: To show recognition of individuals, an octopus must treat one person differently from others who look alike. D describes exactly that: it targets one caretaker among people in identical uniforms. Distractors: A, C, and B show other behaviors but not recognition of specific humans.
choices: Octopuses in the lab change color more often at night than during the day, especially when caretakers are present.
Octopuses in the wild are known to avoid areas where many divers swim, especially during the breeding season.
Octopuses in the lab learned to open jars to reach food inside, sometimes faster than their caretakers expected.
An octopus squirted water at one caretaker who had poked it with a brush, but not at others in the same uniform.

paras: Economist Laila Haddad claims that a minimum wage increase in the city of Lakeport did not lead restaurants to cut jobs, as some business owners had predicted.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Haddad's claim?
byHand: Haddad claims the increase didn't cause restaurants to cut jobs. If restaurant employment stayed about the same afterward, that supports her claim, so B is right. Distractors: A concerns prices, C concerns workers' preferences, and D compares business openings in another city, which doesn't address job cuts in Lakeport.
choices: Restaurant owners in Lakeport raised menu prices slightly in the months after the wage increase.
Restaurant employment in Lakeport stayed about the same for two years after the increase.
Many Lakeport restaurant workers said they preferred higher wages even if it meant fewer hours.
Restaurants in a nearby city opened at a faster rate than restaurants in Lakeport did after the increase.

paras: In his poem "Winter Orchard," Tomas Ivers expresses a sense of hope even as he describes a bleak scene.

stem: Which quotation from "Winter Orchard" most effectively illustrates the claim?
byHand: The claim requires both a bleak scene and a sense of hope. B describes bare, frosted trees and then the buds waiting, small and green, a sign of coming spring. Distractors: A, C, and D describe only bleakness.
choices: "The branches stand like bones against the sky, / and every bird has fled."
"The trees are bare and black with frost, / yet in each twig the buds wait, small and green."
"I walked the rows where once the apples hung, / and found the ground was hard."
"The farmer's house is dark tonight; / no smoke climbs from the chimney."

paras: Geologist Nadia Petrov hypothesizes that a particular valley was carved by a glacier rather than by a river. Glaciers tend to produce U-shaped valleys with wide, flat floors, while rivers tend to produce narrower V-shaped valleys.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Petrov's hypothesis?
byHand: According to the text, glaciers produce U-shaped valleys with wide, flat floors. A valley whose steep sides curve to a broad, flat floor fits that description, so C is right. Distractors: A could suggest a river origin; B concerns present-day plants; D concerns the age of the rocks, not the valley's shape.
choices: A small river currently flows along the bottom of the valley.
The valley contains many species of trees that grow in cold climates.
The valley has steep sides that curve down to a broad, flat floor.
The valley's rocks are older than those in a nearby canyon.

paras: Sociologist Grace Odum argues that public libraries serve as important social spaces, not just places to borrow books. In a survey of library visitors, she asked about their reasons for visiting.

stem: Which finding from the survey, if true, would most directly support Odum's argument?
byHand: Odum argues libraries are social spaces, not only places to borrow books. Visitors who come to attend events, meet friends, or be around others support that view, so A is right. Distractors: B and C focus on books; D concerns where visitors live.
choices: Many visitors said they came mainly to attend events, meet friends, or be around others.
Most visitors said they borrowed at least one book or movie during each visit to the library.
Visitors rated the library's book collection as above average compared with nearby libraries.
Most visitors lived within two miles of the library and walked there rather than driving.

paras: Some researchers have suggested that the decline of a lizard species on a Caribbean island is caused mainly by an invasive snake that preys on the lizards. Ecologist Marco Reyes doubts this explanation.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the explanation that Reyes doubts?
byHand: If the snake were the main cause, lizards should decline mainly where the snake lives. A sharp decline in areas without the snake undercuts that explanation, so B is right. Distractors: A and D would support the snake explanation; C is too indirect to weaken it.
choices: The invasive snake is known to eat lizards on several other islands.
The lizard population has declined just as sharply in parts of the island where the snake has never been found.
The lizard species is smaller than most lizards the snake eats.
The invasive snake arrived on the island shortly before the lizards began to decline.

passage.text: The following text is from a 1920s play. The character Ruth is speaking to her brother.

paras: In the play, Ruth expresses frustration that her brother never takes her ambitions seriously.

stem: Which quotation from the play most effectively illustrates the claim?
byHand: The claim is that Ruth is frustrated because her brother doesn't take her ambitions seriously. In B, she complains that he laughs whenever she says she plans to study law. Distractors: A describes tiredness, C passes along a message, and D compliments him.
choices: "I've been working at the shop every day this week, from seven in the morning until dark, and my feet ache."
"Every time I tell you I mean to study law, you laugh as though I'd said I meant to fly to the moon."
"Mother says supper will be ready at six, so don't be late again, and wash your hands before you sit down."
"You were always the clever one when we were children."

paras: Paleontologists debate whether certain feathered dinosaurs could fly or only glide. Researcher Sophie Laurent argues that one species, which had long feathers on all four limbs, could achieve powered flight rather than just gliding from trees.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Laurent's argument?
byHand: Laurent argues for powered flight, which requires flapping. Shoulder joints capable of the upstroke needed for flapping directly support that, so A is right. Distractors: C fits gliding from trees; B points toward gliding; D concerns size, which doesn't distinguish flying from gliding.
choices: The species' shoulder joints allowed the full upstroke that flapping flight requires.
The species' feathers were arranged in patterns similar to those of modern gliding animals.
Fossils of the species have been found in areas that were once heavily forested.
The species was smaller than most other feathered dinosaurs of its time.

paras: Many researchers assume that the songs of humpback whales change gradually as individual whales improvise. Marine biologist Ellen Garland has proposed that songs can also change suddenly, when an entirely new song spreads from one population to another and replaces the old one.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Garland's proposal?
byHand: Garland proposes that a whole new song can spread from one population to another and replace the old one. D describes a population quickly switching to a neighboring population's song. Distractors: A describes song sharing within a group, not replacement; B describes the gradual change the text says researchers already assume; C shows songs carry far but not that they replace one another.
choices: Humpback whales in a single population all sing nearly the same song as one another in any given season.
Individual humpback whales add small variations to their songs, which change gradually over several years.
Humpback whale songs can be heard by other whales many miles away.
Within one season, a population abandoned its song for one first recorded in a neighboring population.

paras: Historian Amelia Cho argues that in the 1800s, many women in the United States participated in scientific work even though they were largely excluded from universities and professional societies. She points to the widespread practice of collecting and describing plants.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Cho's argument?
byHand: Cho argues that women participated in science despite exclusion from institutions. If women's specimens and descriptions were used in published studies, that shows real scientific contribution, so A is right. Distractors: B confirms exclusion but not participation; C shows botany was socially acceptable, not that women's work was scientific; D concerns admission to universities, which doesn't support the claim about women outside them.
choices: Many specimens in 1800s botanical collections were gathered by women whose descriptions appeared in published studies.
Professional botanical societies of the 1800s admitted very few women as members.
Botany was widely considered a suitable hobby for women in the 1800s because it involved spending time outdoors and studying nature.
Several universities in the United States began admitting women to their science programs in the late 1800s and early 1900s.

paras: A team of psychologists hypothesized that people judge the honesty of a statement partly by how easy it is to read: statements printed in clear, high-contrast fonts will seem more truthful than identical statements printed in faint, hard-to-read fonts.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's hypothesis?
byHand: The hypothesis is about judgments of truth. D shows that identical statements were judged true more often in easy-to-read fonts. Distractors: A shows reading speed but not judgments of truth; B concerns memory; C concerns preference, not belief.
choices: Participants read statements printed in high-contrast fonts faster than the same statements printed in faint fonts.
Participants remembered statements printed in faint fonts better than statements printed in high-contrast fonts.
Participants said that they preferred high-contrast fonts to faint fonts when reading for long periods of time.
Participants rated identical statements as true more often in high-contrast fonts than in faint ones.

paras: Ecologist Ravi Menon claims that the presence of wolves in a national park indirectly helped streamside willow trees recover. According to Menon, wolves caused elk to avoid areas near streams where they could easily be ambushed, so the elk browsed less on young willows there.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Menon's claim?
byHand: Menon's claim depends on elk avoiding streams because of wolves. C shows elk didn't avoid streams and points to another cause (wetter conditions) for the willows' recovery, which undercuts his explanation. Distractors: A is consistent with his claim; B could fit his claim or another explanation; D doesn't address elk behavior near streams.
choices: Willows near the park's streams grew taller and more plentiful in the years after wolves were reintroduced.
Elk populations in the park declined somewhat in the years after wolves were reintroduced, then leveled off.
Elk visited streams as often after wolves returned, and willows recovered only where streams got wetter.
Wolves in the park hunted deer and bison as well as elk.

paras: In the essay "On Walking," the fictional essayist Margaret Vane argues that walking without a destination allows a person to notice details that hurried travelers miss.

stem: Which quotation from "On Walking" most effectively illustrates Vane's argument?
byHand: Vane's argument links aimless walking to noticing details hurried people miss. In C, having nowhere to be, she notices a spider repairing its web that a hundred commuters passed by. Distractors: A concerns pleasant routes, B familiarity, and D how often people drive. None connects aimless walking with noticing overlooked details.
choices: "The shortest route between two points is rarely the most pleasant one."
"I have walked these streets for thirty years, in every season and at every hour, and I know each one by name and by sound."
"Having nowhere to be, I stopped to watch a spider mend its web, a thing a hundred commuters had passed without a glance."
"Many people now drive to places that are only a few minutes away on foot."

paras: Researchers studying a type of bacteria hypothesized that the bacteria use chemical signals to "count" their own numbers and begin producing light only when enough of them are present. They predicted that a small group of the bacteria would glow if exposed to the chemical signal at the concentration normally produced by a large group.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' prediction?
byHand: The prediction is specifically that a small group will glow if given the chemical at a large group's concentration. A reports that result. Distractors: B concerns time of day; C shows small groups don't glow normally, which is expected but doesn't test the prediction; D shows large groups produce more chemical, which fits the hypothesis but doesn't test what happens when a small group receives it.
choices: A small group began glowing once the signaling chemical was added at a high concentration.
A large group of the bacteria glowed more brightly at night than during the day.
A small group of the bacteria did not glow when no signaling chemical was added to their container.
A large group of the bacteria produced more of the signaling chemical than a small group did.

paras: Literary scholar Nikhil Bose argues that the novelist Clara Weld used weather to mirror her characters' emotions, but only in her later novels; in her early work, Bose claims, weather is described in purely practical terms.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Bose's argument?
byHand: Bose claims weather mirrors emotion only in Weld's later novels. A storm in her first novel explicitly matched to the heroine's fury directly contradicts that, so B is right. Distractors: A and D are consistent with his argument; C concerns Weld's life, not her writing.
choices: Weld's later novels contain many more descriptions of weather than her early novels, which focus mostly on farm life.
In Weld's first novel, a storm breaks out as the heroine learns of a betrayal, its thunder likened to her fury.
Weld wrote her early novels while living in a region known for mild weather.
Several critics have praised the descriptions of weather in Weld's later novels.

paras: Economists studying small farms in a mountain region claim that farmers who received weather forecasts by text message planted at better times and therefore harvested more crops than farmers who did not receive the forecasts.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the economists' claim?
byHand: The claim attributes higher harvests to forecasts. If forecast recipients also received better seeds and more fertilizer, those advantages could explain the larger harvests instead, weakening the claim. A is right. Distractors: C supports the claim; B affected all farmers; D concerns phone ownership, which doesn't offer another explanation for the difference.
choices: Farmers who got the forecasts were also, on average, given better seeds and more fertilizer.
The region experienced unusually heavy rainfall during the study.
Farmers who received the text messages said they found the forecasts useful.
Most farmers in the region already owned mobile phones and used them daily before the study began.

paras: Art historian Jonas Becker claims that a portrait long attributed to the painter Hendrik Vos was actually painted by one of Vos's students. Becker notes that Vos always prepared his canvases with a gray base layer, while his students typically used a reddish-brown one.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Becker's claim?
byHand: Becker's evidence depends on base layers: Vos used gray, his students reddish-brown. Finding a reddish-brown layer under the portrait supports the student attribution, so D is right. Distractors: A, B, and C would, if anything, support the traditional attribution to Vos.
choices: The portrait's subject is known to have visited Vos's studio several times.
The portrait is signed with a signature resembling Vos's.
The portrait was sold by a dealer who handled many of Vos's paintings.
Scientific analysis shows that the portrait was painted over a reddish-brown base layer.

paras: Some linguists claim that the word order of a language influences how its speakers remember events. In a study, speakers of a language that typically places the person performing an action first ("The girl kicked the ball") and speakers of a language that typically places the object first watched short videos of accidental and intentional actions.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the linguists' claim?
byHand: The claim is that word order affects memory of events. B shows a memory difference between the two groups that matches the first language's focus on who acts. Distractors: A shows no difference between groups; C concerns length of description, and D concerns enjoyment, neither of which is memory.
choices: Both groups remembered intentional actions better than accidental ones.
Speakers of the first language more often remembered who performed accidental actions.
Speakers of both languages described the videos using a similar number of words.
Speakers of the second language were more likely to say they had enjoyed watching the videos.

paras: Urban ecologist Teresa Lindqvist claims that green roofs, rooftops covered with plants, can lower the temperature of the buildings beneath them during summer.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lindqvist's claim?
byHand: The claim is about lowering building temperatures in summer. D compares top-floor temperatures on hot days and shows that buildings with green roofs were cooler. Distractors: A concerns cost, B appearance, and C habitat, none of which addresses temperature.
choices: Green roofs are more expensive to install than ordinary roofs.
Many people say they enjoy the appearance of green roofs.
Green roofs can provide habitat for birds and insects in cities.
On hot days, the top floors of buildings with green roofs were several degrees cooler than the top floors of similar buildings with ordinary roofs.

paras: Some nutrition experts recommend that people eat breakfast every day. They argue that a morning meal provides energy for the day and helps people avoid overeating later.

Recent studies have found that skipping breakfast doesn't necessarily lead people to eat more at lunch or dinner. For some people, eating breakfast simply adds calories to the day without making them less hungry later.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the experts' argument in Text 1?
byHand: Text 1's experts say breakfast helps people avoid overeating later; Text 2 reports that skipping breakfast doesn't necessarily lead to eating more later. A captures that challenge. Distractors: B contradicts Text 2; C and D introduce claims neither text makes.
choices: By pointing out that eating breakfast may not prevent overeating later in the day
By agreeing that breakfast is the most important meal of the day
By arguing that people should eat larger lunches and dinners
By claiming that many common breakfast foods contain too much sugar to provide lasting energy

paras: Many city planners believe that adding more lanes to busy highways will reduce traffic jams. More lanes, they argue, give cars more room and allow traffic to move faster.
Researchers have repeatedly found that when highways are widened, traffic soon returns to its old levels. The extra space encourages more people to drive, so the new lanes fill up within a few years.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the planners' belief in Text 1?
byHand: The planners say more lanes reduce jams; the researchers found that new lanes attract more drivers and fill up, so any benefit fades (B). Distractors: A contradicts Text 2; C goes beyond Text 2, which doesn't recommend fewer lanes; D introduces a cause neither text mentions.
choices: They would agree that wider highways permanently reduce traffic jams.
They would argue that the benefits of extra lanes fade as more people drive.
They would claim that highways should have fewer lanes than they do now to discourage driving.
They would suggest that traffic jams are caused mainly by accidents rather than by too few lanes.

paras: Homework helps students practice what they learn in class. Teachers who assign regular homework report that their students remember lessons better and come to class better prepared.

While some homework can be useful, research suggests that its benefits are small for young children. For elementary school students, a short assignment or reading at home is often just as helpful as a long one.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
byHand: Text 1 praises homework, and Text 2 says "some homework can be useful," so both would agree it can have value (C). Distractors: A and B conflict with one text or the other; D is too extreme for either text.
choices: Homework should be eliminated in elementary schools.
Long homework assignments are the most helpful kind.
Homework can have some value for students.
Students who don't do homework never remember their lessons.

paras: Zoos play an important role in protecting endangered species. Breeding programs at zoos have helped save animals such as the California condor, which was nearly extinct in the 1980s.
Critics argue that zoos keep animals in small spaces that can't match their natural habitats. They point out that some large animals, such as elephants, show signs of stress in captivity.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the critics in Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?
byHand: Text 1 praises zoos' conservation role; the critics in Text 2 focus on the stress and limited space that captivity creates, so they'd say Text 1 overlooks those costs (D). Distractors: A goes beyond Text 2, which doesn't deny that breeding programs work; B contradicts the critics; C isn't discussed.
choices: They would argue that zoo breeding programs have never helped any species.
They would agree that zoos are the best place for all animals to live.
They would say that the California condor is not truly endangered.
They would say that the claim overlooks the harm captivity can do to some animals.

paras: Electric cars produce no exhaust while driving, so they can greatly reduce air pollution in cities. Switching to electric cars is one of the best ways to make city air cleaner.

Electric cars are only as clean as the electricity that powers them. In regions where most electricity comes from burning coal, charging an electric car still causes pollution, although it occurs at the power plant rather than on the street.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Text 1?
byHand: Text 2 says electric cars are only as clean as their electricity source, which complicates Text 1's broad claim, so B is right. Distractors: A contradicts both texts; C contradicts Text 2; D introduces a proposal neither text makes.
choices: By arguing that electric cars produce more exhaust than gasoline cars when driven in cities
By noting that the benefit of electric cars depends on how their electricity is produced
By agreeing that electric cars cause no pollution of any kind, on the street or anywhere else
By claiming that cities should ban all cars

paras: Reading on paper helps people understand and remember what they read. In several studies, students who read printed texts answered more comprehension questions correctly than students who read the same texts on screens.
Screens are not necessarily worse for reading. When students were taught to read slowly and take notes while reading on a screen, their comprehension matched that of students reading on paper.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the studies described in Text 1?
byHand: Text 2 found that with good reading habits, screen comprehension matched paper, suggesting the Text 1 difference depends on how students read (D). Distractors: A and B aren't supported; C overstates Text 2, which found the two equal, not paper worse.
choices: By claiming that the studies were never conducted
By agreeing that screens should never be used for reading
By arguing that printed texts are actually harder to understand than the same texts read on screens
By suggesting that the difference may depend on how students read on screens, not on screens

paras: Many people believe that cracking your knuckles causes arthritis, a condition that makes joints painful and stiff.
One doctor cracked the knuckles on only one of his hands for more than sixty years. At the end of that time, neither hand had arthritis, and there was no difference between them.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief described in Text 1?
byHand: The doctor's experiment showed no arthritis in either hand after decades of cracking one, which casts doubt on the belief (D). Distractors: A contradicts that evidence; B and C aren't supported by either text.
choices: By agreeing that knuckle cracking is a major cause of arthritis
By arguing that people should crack their knuckles more often
By suggesting that arthritis affects only the left hand
By presenting evidence that casts doubt on the belief

paras: Learning to play a musical instrument can improve children's skills in other subjects. Several studies have found that children who take music lessons score higher on math tests than children who don't.

Children who take music lessons often come from families that can afford other advantages, such as tutoring and books. These advantages, rather than the lessons themselves, may explain why music students score higher on math tests.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion in Text 1?
byHand: Text 2 proposes that family advantages, not lessons, may explain the scores, so it offers another explanation for the same finding (A). Distractors: B contradicts Text 2; C isn't claimed; D contradicts Text 2, which accepts that music students score higher.
choices: By suggesting that other factors could explain the higher math scores
By agreeing that music lessons directly improve math skills
By arguing that music lessons harm children's math skills
By claiming that children who take music lessons don't score higher in math

paras: Many archaeologists believe that the earliest people to reach the Americas walked across a land bridge connecting Siberia and Alaska about 13,000 years ago, then traveled south through an ice-free corridor in what is now Canada.

Evidence from sites in Chile and Oregon shows that people were living in the Americas more than 14,000 years ago, before the ice-free corridor opened. Some researchers therefore propose that early migrants traveled by boat along the Pacific coast.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the view described in Text 1?
byHand: Text 2 cites sites older than the corridor's opening, which challenges the idea that migrants arrived only through it (A). Distractors: B contradicts Text 2; C mentions the Atlantic, which isn't discussed; D contradicts Text 2's evidence.
choices: They would argue that some early sites are too old for people to have arrived only through the corridor.
They would agree that the ice-free corridor was the only possible route.
They would claim that people first reached the Americas by crossing the Atlantic Ocean from Europe by boat.
They would argue that no people lived anywhere in the Americas before about 13,000 years ago, when the corridor opened.

paras: Social media has made teenagers lonelier. As young people spend more time scrolling through feeds, they spend less time with friends in person, and surveys show rising rates of loneliness among teens.

The relationship between social media and loneliness is more complicated than it first appears. Psychologist Kira Lund found that teens who used social media mainly to chat with friends they already knew reported feeling less lonely, while those who mostly scrolled through strangers' posts reported feeling more lonely.

stem: Based on the texts, how would Lund (Text 2) most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?
byHand: Lund found different effects for chatting with friends and scrolling strangers' posts, so the effect depends on how teens use social media (C). Distractors: A ignores the positive finding; B ignores that both kinds of use affected loneliness; D isn't discussed.
choices: She would agree that all social media use makes teenagers lonelier.
She would argue that social media has no effect on loneliness.
She would say that the effect of social media may depend on how teenagers use it.
She would claim that teenagers spend more time with friends in person than they did in the past.

paras: The fictional scholar Henry Cole argues that Shakespeare's plays should always be performed in Elizabethan costumes and settings. Only by recreating the original context, he says, can audiences understand what Shakespeare intended.

Director Amara Diallo stages Shakespeare in modern settings, with characters in business suits or military uniforms. She argues that the plays' themes of power, love, and betrayal are timeless and that modern settings help audiences see their relevance.

stem: Based on the texts, how would Diallo (Text 2) most likely respond to Cole's argument in Text 1?
byHand: Cole says only the original setting reveals Shakespeare's intent; Diallo argues that the themes are timeless and that modern settings show their relevance, so she'd disagree (D). Distractors: A contradicts her view; B and C introduce claims neither text makes.
choices: She would agree that modern settings confuse audiences who are new to Shakespeare.
She would argue that Shakespeare's plays shouldn't be performed at all in theaters today.
She would claim that Elizabethan costumes and settings are too expensive to produce well.
She would argue that audiences can grasp the plays without the original setting.

paras: For many years, scientists believed that the dinosaurs were wiped out by a single catastrophe: the impact of a huge asteroid in what is now Mexico about 66 million years ago.

Some geologists point out that around the same time, massive volcanic eruptions in what is now India released enormous amounts of gas into the atmosphere. They argue that these eruptions had already stressed many species before the asteroid struck.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the geologists in Text 2 most likely view the explanation in Text 1?
byHand: The geologists add the volcanic eruptions as an earlier stress on species but don't deny the asteroid, so they'd see Text 1's explanation as incomplete (A). Distractors: B and D contradict Text 2's acceptance of the asteroid's timing; C contradicts their argument about the eruptions.
choices: As incomplete, because it leaves out another possible factor in the extinction
As completely wrong, because no asteroid struck Earth 66 million years ago
As correct, because volcanic eruptions had no effect on dinosaurs
As irrelevant, because dinosaurs died out long before the asteroid struck

paras: The fictional economist Jonas Weber argues that a four-day workweek would hurt businesses. With one fewer day of work, he says, employees would simply get less done, reducing companies' output.

In a trial involving dozens of companies, employees who switched to a four-day week without a pay cut maintained their productivity. Many reported feeling less tired and more focused, and most companies chose to keep the shorter schedule after the trial ended.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Weber's argument in Text 1?
byHand: Weber predicts lower output; Text 2 reports that productivity stayed the same in the trial, so the author would counter with that evidence (B). Distractors: A contradicts Text 2; C and D aren't supported.
choices: By agreeing that employees inevitably get less done when they work fewer days per week
By pointing to evidence that output need not fall when the workweek is shortened
By arguing that employees should work six days a week
By claiming that companies in the trial lost money even though productivity stayed the same

paras: Many birdwatchers believe that feeding wild birds in winter helps them survive cold months when food is scarce.

A study in Britain found that bird feeders benefited some common species, such as blue tits, which became more numerous. But the same study found that feeders may also help these species outcompete rarer birds that don't visit feeders, potentially reducing the number of those rarer species.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief in Text 1?
byHand: Text 2 reports that feeders help common species but may hurt rarer ones through competition, a mixed picture (C). Distractors: A and B misrepresent Text 2's findings; D ignores the risk to rarer birds.
choices: By arguing that bird feeders harm all species of birds, common and rare alike
By claiming that bird feeders have no real effect on wild birds in winter
By noting that feeders may help some species but risk harming others
By agreeing that feeders are always beneficial for wild birds in cold months

paras: Standardized test scores are a fair way to compare college applicants. Because every student takes the same test under the same conditions, the scores give admissions officers an objective measure.

Although students take the same test, they don't prepare under the same conditions. Students whose families can pay for tutoring and multiple attempts often score higher, so test scores can reflect differences in resources as well as in ability.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 that test scores are an objective measure?
byHand: Text 1 emphasizes identical testing conditions; Text 2 points out unequal preparation, which means scores can reflect resources, not only ability (B). Distractors: A contradicts Text 2; C misreads Text 2, which accepts that students take the same test; D isn't discussed.
choices: By agreeing that test scores reflect only students' abilities
By arguing that differences in preparation can affect scores, complicating their objectivity
By claiming that standardized tests are given under different conditions in different places
By suggesting that admissions officers ignore test scores

paras: Ancient Romans built long aqueducts to bring fresh water into their cities. Historians often present these structures as a sign of Rome's devotion to public health.

Historian Lucia Ferro notes that much of the water carried by aqueducts went to public baths, fountains, and the private homes of the wealthy. In her view, aqueducts served as displays of power and status at least as much as they served public health.

stem: Based on the texts, how would Ferro (Text 2) most likely respond to the historians' view in Text 1?
byHand: Ferro argues that aqueducts were also displays of power and status, adding purposes the Text 1 view overlooks (A). Distractors: D and C contradict the texts; B contradicts her emphasis on other purposes.
choices: She would suggest that the view overlooks other important purposes of aqueducts.
She would agree that aqueducts were built mainly to protect public health.
She would claim that aqueducts carried water only to farms outside the cities.
She would argue that Romans didn't build aqueducts.

paras: Some researchers have warned that the use of calculators in elementary school prevents children from learning basic arithmetic.

A review of more than fifty studies found that when calculators were used alongside traditional instruction, children's arithmetic skills were not harmed, and their problem-solving skills often improved.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the authors of the review in Text 2 most likely respond to the warning in Text 1?
byHand: The review found no harm to arithmetic skills when calculators accompanied traditional teaching, which counters the warning (A). Distractors: B contradicts the review; C and D misrepresent it.
choices: By presenting evidence that calculators used with traditional instruction need not harm arithmetic
By agreeing that calculators should be banned in elementary schools until children master arithmetic
By arguing that children should learn only problem-solving skills
By claiming that traditional instruction is harmful to children

paras: Many scientists believed that humans are the only animals that recognize themselves in mirrors. In tests, most animals treat their reflection as another animal.

Researchers have found that some fish, called cleaner wrasse, appear to pass the mirror test. When a colored mark was placed on their throats, visible only in a mirror, the fish tried to scrape it off after seeing their reflection.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the belief described in Text 1?
byHand: The wrasse's response to the mark suggests self-recognition in a non-human animal, which challenges the belief (B). Distractors: A contradicts the evidence; C contradicts Text 2's use of the test with fish; D overstates. Text 2 discusses one species.
choices: By agreeing that only humans can recognize themselves in mirrors
By presenting evidence that at least one other animal may recognize itself
By arguing that mirror tests cannot be used with fish
By claiming that most animals pass the mirror test easily

paras: Remote work is bad for creativity. When employees work from home, they miss the chance encounters in hallways and break rooms that often spark new ideas.
